title: Kartoffelbrot
subtitle: German potato bread that stays moist for several days thanks to the starch in the potato
excerpt: Kartoffelbrot stays moist for three to four days where a lean bread would be stale by day two. The cooked potato adds gelatinised starch that binds water in the crumb, lowers the effective gluten percentage of the dough, and gives a slight sweetness. It is a forgiving dough that handles well and rises well.
sourceNotes: Kartoffelbrot (potato bread) has been baked across Germany for centuries, particularly in northern and central regions where potato farming is widespread. The bread uses cooked, mashed potato worked into a yeasted wheat dough. Its extended shelf life and soft crumb have been documented in German bread-baking literature, including the work of baking researchers at institutions such as the German Bread Institute.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice before freezing for easier use. Freeze in a bag for up to 3 months. Toast from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can cold-proof overnight in the fridge after shaping. Bake straight from the fridge the next morning, adding 5 minutes to the baking time.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 220 degrees Celsius. Place a roasting pan of hot water on the bottom shelf for the first 15 minutes to create steam and a good crust.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cooked, mashed potato worked into a bread dough contributes gelatinised starch. This starch binds water in the crumb and slows staling, giving the loaf a noticeably longer shelf life than a plain flour-and-water dough. The potato also softens the crumb texture and adds a slight natural sweetness.

content.text: is what keeps kartoffelbrot soft for days after baking. Use floury potatoes (King Edward, Maris Piper) that break down when cooked; waxy varieties stay dense in the dough. Cool the mashed potato completely before adding it; hot potato kills the yeast.

items.prepNote: floury variety, boiled and mashed smooth, cooled completely

content.text: Combine the flour, yeast, and salt. Add the mashed potato and work it into the flour with your fingers until the mixture resembles rough breadcrumbs. Add the warm water and olive oil and bring the dough together.

Knead for 8 minutes. The potato makes the dough softer and slightly stickier than a plain bread dough; use a bench scraper to help rather than adding more flour. The dough is ready when smooth and no longer tearing when stretched.
Cover and leave at room temperature for 1 hour until doubled.
Turn the dough out and shape into a log for a loaf tin, or a tight round for free-form baking. Place in a greased loaf tin or on a lined baking tray. Cover and proof for 45 minutes until well puffed.

Preheat the oven to 220 degrees Celsius with a roasting pan on the bottom shelf. Score the top of the loaf with a sharp knife or lame. Pour a cup of hot water into the roasting pan as the bread goes in to generate steam.

Bake for 15 minutes, then remove the water pan and reduce the oven to 200 degrees Celsius. Bake for a further 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden. The loaf is done when it sounds hollow when tapped on the base.
The water drained from cooked potatoes contains dissolved starch. Use it instead of plain water in the dough for an even softer crumb. Cool it first so it does not kill the yeast.
